4010:
To deem something means to consider it, judge it, or conclude that it is a certain way. When you deem something, you are forming a firm opinion or an official judgment about it — deciding in your mind (or in an authoritative capacity) that something is a particular thing or falls into a particular category.

Think of it this way: you look at a situation, weigh it in your mind, and arrive at a settled conclusion. That act of arriving at a conclusion and treating something as being a certain way — that is "deeming."

This is important: deem is a formal word. You would not use it in casual conversation with a friend. You would not say, "I deem this pizza delicious." It would sound strange and stiff.

Instead, deem is used in serious, official, or formal contexts — in legal documents, government policies, academic writing, professional settings, and formal speech. It often suggests that the person making the judgment has some authority or responsibility to make that judgment. It carries a sense of weight and finality. The judgment has been made; it is not casual or tentative.
How It Works in a Sentence

Deem almost always follows one of these patterns:

Pattern 1: deem + object + adjective
This is the most common structure. Someone judges the object to have a certain quality.

  • "The committee deemed the proposal unacceptable." (The committee judged the proposal to be unacceptable.)
  • "The judge deemed the evidence sufficient." (The judge concluded that the evidence was enough.)
  • "The manager deemed the employee's conduct inappropriate."

Pattern 2: deem + object + noun
Someone judges the object to be a certain thing.

  • "The board deemed her the most qualified candidate."
  • "The court deemed him a flight risk."

Pattern 3: deem it + adjective + to do something
This structure is very common in formal writing. "It" here is a placeholder.

  • "I deem it necessary to inform you of this change."
  • "They deemed it appropriate to postpone the meeting."
  • "She deemed it wise to consult a lawyer."

One of the most frequent ways you will encounter "deem" is in the passive voice: to be deemed. This is extremely common in legal, official, and formal writing.

  • "The contract was deemed invalid."
  • "The area has been deemed unsafe for public access."
  • "Any late submissions will be deemed unacceptable."
  • "He was deemed fit to stand trial."

In these sentences, someone in authority has made a judgment, and the result of that judgment is what matters. The passive form puts the focus on the thing being judged, not on who is doing the judging.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Deem vs. Think: "Think" is casual and personal. "I think it's a bad idea" is an everyday opinion. "I deem it a bad idea" sounds overly formal and is almost never said in conversation. The key difference is register — think is everyday, deem is formal and deliberate.

Deem vs. Consider: These are close in meaning. "Consider" can mean either to think carefully about something (before deciding) or to regard something as being a certain way. "Deem" only carries the second meaning — the concluded judgment. Also, "deem" feels slightly more authoritative and final than "consider." When a court deems something, it sounds more decisive than when it merely considers something.

Deem vs. Find: In legal settings, "find" and "deem" can overlap. A jury finds someone guilty; a court deems a policy unconstitutional. Both imply an official conclusion, but "find" is more tied to factual verdicts, while "deem" leans more toward classification, qualification, or characterization.

Deem vs. Regard: "Regard" means to see or think of something in a certain way and can be used more broadly and informally. "Deem" is more formal and implies a more deliberate, often authoritative decision.

Many learners write "deemed as" — for example, "The plan was deemed as too risky." This is incorrect in standard English. You do not need "as" after deem. The correct form is simply "The plan was deemed too risky." Drop the "as."
Where You Will See This Word

You will most often encounter "deem" in:

  • Legal writing — court opinions, laws, contracts, regulations
  • Official policies — school handbooks, company policies, government rules
  • Formal journalism — serious newspaper editorials and reports
  • Academic writing — research papers, formal essays
  • Formal speech — official announcements, speeches

If you had to remember one thing: to deem something is to officially or deliberately judge that it is a certain way. It is a word of formal, considered judgment — often made by someone with authority — and it signals that a conclusion has been firmly reached.

Whenever you see it, ask yourself: Who is making a judgment here, and what are they concluding? Answer those two questions, and the meaning of "deem" in that sentence will be clear every time.
4011: Deep means going far from the surface toward the inside or the bottom. This is the single idea that connects almost every use of this word. Whether you're talking about water, feelings, sleep, or thinking — "deep" always points to something that goes far beyond what you can see or touch on the outside.
1. Physical: Far Down From the Top

The most basic meaning. If something is deep, there is a lot of distance between its surface and its bottom.

  • A deep well — the water is very far below the ground.
  • A deep river — you cannot touch the bottom with your feet.
  • A deep cut on the skin — it goes far below the surface.
  • A deep bowl — it can hold a lot because it is not shallow.

The opposite is shallow (not going far down).

You also use it to say how far down something goes:

  • "The lake is 200 meters deep."
  • "The snow was knee-deep." (It reached up to my knees.)
2. Physical: Far From the Front or the Outside

"Deep" can also describe distance from the front edge or the opening of something — going far inward.

  • A deep cupboard — you have to reach far in to get things at the back.
  • Deep in the forest — far from the edge of the forest, surrounded by trees on all sides.
  • Deep in the mountains — far from towns and roads.
  • The treasure was hidden deep inside the cave.
3. Sound: Low in Pitch

A deep voice or sound is low — it vibrates slowly, producing a heavy, bass-like quality. Think of a big drum, a lion's roar, or a large man's voice.

  • He had a deep, powerful voice that filled the room.
  • The bell made a deep, slow sound.
  • A deep growl came from the dog's throat.

The opposite here is high-pitched.
4. Color: Strong, Rich, and Dark

A deep color is not pale or light. It is rich, strong, and full — like the color has a lot of intensity packed into it.

  • Deep red — like dark wine or blood.
  • Deep blue — like the color of the ocean on a clear day.
  • Deep green — like the dark leaves of a pine tree.
  • She wore a deep purple dress.

The opposite would be a light shade or a pale color.
5. Emotion and Experience: Intense and Strong

When feelings, states, or experiences are described as "deep," it means they are not small or surface-level — they go far inside a person and are very strong.

  • Deep love — love that is very powerful and sincere, not casual.
  • Deep sorrow — extreme sadness that hurts greatly.
  • Deep joy — a very strong feeling of happiness.
  • He was in a deep sleep — he was sleeping so heavily that it would be hard to wake him up.
  • She was in deep trouble — serious, not minor trouble.
  • There was a deep silence in the room — total, heavy silence.
6. Knowledge and Thinking: Profound and Serious

When something involves serious, careful thought — or when someone understands a subject very thoroughly — we call it "deep." This is about going beneath the surface of a topic, the same way physical "deep" means going below the surface of water.

  • A deep thinker — someone who thinks about things carefully, seriously, and at a level most people don't reach.
  • Deep knowledge — thorough understanding, not just the basics.
  • A deep question — a question that is difficult to answer and requires serious thought (e.g., "Why do we exist?").
  • That book is very deep — it has complex, layered ideas that take time to understand.
  • He has a deep understanding of mathematics.

The opposite would be shallow or superficial understanding.
7. Absorbed in Something: Fully Involved

When someone is deep in something, their mind is fully inside it. They are so involved or focused that they are not paying attention to anything else.

  • She was deep in thought — completely absorbed in her thinking, unaware of what was around her.
  • They were deep in conversation — so engaged in talking that they noticed nothing else.
  • He was deep in debt — seriously involved in a financial problem with a lot of debt piled up.
  • She was deep in her work.
8. Hidden, Secret, or Not Easily Seen

"Deep" can describe something that lies underneath the visible surface — something that is not obvious or is kept carefully hidden.

  • A deep secret — a secret that is very carefully guarded and not known to others.
  • His deep feelings — the emotions he keeps hidden inside, not shown to others.
  • There is a deep meaning in this poem — a meaning that is not immediately obvious; you have to think hard to discover it.
  • Something deep inside her told her it was wrong — a strong inner feeling, not something visible on the surface.
9. Far Into Time or Space

"Deep" is used to describe being far into a period of time or a region of space — the same idea of distance, just applied to time or location.

  • Deep into the night — very late at night, long after midnight.
  • Deep in winter — in the coldest, most intense part of winter.
  • Deep in the past — a long time ago.
  • Deep space — the vast, distant regions of the universe, far from Earth.
10. In Sports: Far Back From the Attacking Area

In sports like football (soccer), cricket, or baseball, "deep" refers to a position or location that is far from where scoring or attacking usually happens.

  • The fielder was placed deep — far back, near the boundary.
  • He was defending deep in his own half — far back, near his own goal.
Putting It All Together

The single thread through every meaning of deep is: going far from the surface, the edge, or the top. Whether it's a deep hole, a deep voice, deep sleep, deep knowledge, or deep space — something "deep" always has more to it than what is immediately visible or accessible. It goes further inward, further down, further in, or further beneath the obvious.

Think of it this way: anything "deep" makes you work harder to reach its full extent — whether physically, emotionally, or intellectually. That is the soul of the word.
4012:
A deepfake is a fake photo, video, or audio recording — made using artificial intelligence (AI) — that looks and sounds so realistic that most people cannot tell it is fake.

The word itself is a blend of "deep learning" (a type of AI) and "fake." But don't worry about that — what matters is what the thing is and what it does.

Imagine you have a real video of a news anchor reading the day's headlines. Now imagine someone uses AI to replace that anchor's face with a celebrity's face — perfectly matching the lighting, skin tone, head movements, and even the way the lips move — so the celebrity appears to be saying things they never said, in a video they were never in.

That manipulated video is a deepfake.

More broadly, a deepfake is any piece of media — a video, an image, or an audio clip — in which:

  • A real person's face, voice, or body has been digitally swapped, altered, or entirely fabricated by AI, and
  • The result looks or sounds convincingly real.

The key quality that makes a deepfake dangerous and remarkable is its believability. Unlike older, crude photo edits that are obviously fake, a deepfake can be nearly indistinguishable from the real thing.
How the AI Actually Does This (Simplified)

You don't need to understand the technical details deeply, but a basic sense helps.

The AI is trained by studying thousands of real images or recordings of a person — from different angles, lighting conditions, and expressions. Over time, it learns that person's appearance so thoroughly that it can then generate new images of that person doing or saying things they never actually did.

Think of it like a very advanced art forger. A forger studies a painter's style so deeply — the brushstrokes, the colours, the technique — that they can create a new painting that looks like it came from that painter's hand. The AI does something similar, but with a person's face and voice.

Deepfakes come in several forms:

  • Video deepfakes — The most common type. A person's face is swapped onto someone else's body in a video, or their face is kept but their words or expressions are altered. A famous politician might appear to be giving a speech they never gave.
  • Audio deepfakes (also called voice clones) — Only the voice is faked. The AI mimics a person's tone, accent, and speech patterns so precisely that it can generate speech in their voice saying anything. A son might receive a phone call that sounds exactly like his mother, but it is entirely AI-generated.
  • Image deepfakes — A single still photograph is manipulated or entirely generated. A person might appear in a photo at a place they never visited.
  • Full synthetic deepfakes — The most advanced kind. The person in the video or image does not exist at all. The AI creates a completely fictional human being who looks entirely real.

Deepfakes are made by a wide range of people, for very different reasons — some harmless, some deeply harmful.

Harmless or creative uses:

  • Film and entertainment studios use deepfake-like technology to de-age actors, bring deceased actors back to the screen, or dub films into other languages while matching lip movements.
  • Hobbyists create amusing videos — putting a friend's face onto a movie character, for example.
  • Educators and historians explore "what if" scenarios by recreating historical figures.

Harmful uses:

  • Misinformation and propaganda — Making a world leader appear to declare war, or a candidate appear to say something scandalous, right before an election. These can spread rapidly and cause real-world panic or political damage before the truth catches up.
  • Fraud and scams — Criminals use audio deepfakes to impersonate a CEO calling an employee and ordering an urgent bank transfer. This has already cost real companies millions of dollars.
  • Harassment and reputation destruction — People's faces are placed onto explicit content without their consent. This is overwhelmingly done to women and is a serious form of abuse.
  • Identity fraud — Deepfakes are used to fool identity verification systems, such as the kind that ask you to record yourself turning your head or blinking.
Why Are Deepfakes a Big Problem?

The danger of deepfakes goes beyond any single fake video. They threaten something fundamental: our ability to trust what we see and hear.

For centuries, a video recording or a photograph was considered hard evidence. If you saw something with your own eyes, you believed it. Deepfakes shatter that assumption entirely. Once people know that any video could be fake, two things happen:

  1. False content is believed — People see a convincing deepfake and accept it as real.
  2. True content is doubted — Real, genuine recordings can be dismissed as "probably a deepfake." A politician caught on camera doing something wrong can simply claim the footage is AI-generated. This is sometimes called the liar's dividend — the existence of deepfakes gives bad actors an excuse to deny reality.

Both of these outcomes are dangerous for society.
How Can You Spot a Deepfake?

Spotting deepfakes is getting harder every year as the technology improves, but there are still some clues to watch for, especially in lower-quality deepfakes:

  • Unnatural blinking — Early deepfakes blinked too rarely or in odd ways. Newer ones are better, but eyes can still look slightly glassy or strange.
  • Weird edges around the face — The boundary where the face meets the hair or ears can look blurry, flickery, or slightly mismatched.
  • Inconsistent lighting — The face might be lit differently from the rest of the body or background.
  • Unnatural skin — The skin can look unusually smooth, waxy, or slightly "wrong."
  • Audio-visual mismatch — In video deepfakes, the voice might not perfectly sync with the lips, or the voice might sound slightly robotic or flat.
  • Unnatural head movements — Sudden head turns or jerky movements can reveal manipulation.
  • The "uncanny valley" feeling — You cannot quite explain what is wrong, but something feels off. Trust that instinct.

However, it is important to accept that high-quality deepfakes may not be detectable by the human eye at all. This is why AI-powered detection tools are being actively developed to identify deepfakes automatically.

Deepfakes represent a turning point in human history's relationship with media. For the first time, synthetic content can be as convincing as real content — and the technology to create it is becoming cheaper, faster, and accessible to almost anyone with a computer.

This makes media literacy (the skill of critically evaluating what you see and hear) more important than ever. Before sharing or reacting to a striking video or recording of a public figure, it is wise to ask: Where did this come from? Has a trusted news organisation verified it? Is there any reason someone might want to fake this?

Governments, technology companies, and researchers around the world are actively working on laws, detection tools, and content-labelling systems to fight the misuse of deepfakes. But as of today, it remains one of the most significant challenges in the age of artificial intelligence.

In one sentence: A deepfake is an AI-generated fake video, image, or audio recording that manipulates or fabricates a real person's appearance or voice so convincingly that it is difficult or impossible to distinguish from reality.
4013:
To deface something means to deliberately damage or spoil the way it looks — especially its surface or outward appearance — by marking, scratching, writing, painting, or otherwise messing it up in a way that makes it look ugly, damaged, or difficult to read and recognize.

Think of it this way: the word contains the idea of a face — the visible front of something. To de-face it is to attack or ruin that face.

Defacing is not random destruction. It has three important qualities:

1. It targets appearance, not structure.
When something is defaced, it is not necessarily broken apart or made useless. It is marred — its looks are spoiled. A statue that has been spray-painted with graffiti is still a statue. It is still standing. But it has been defaced.

2. It is almost always deliberate.
People don't accidentally deface things. The act is intentional — someone chose to mark, scratch, or write on something.

3. The thing being defaced usually has value, dignity, or public importance.
You typically hear "deface" used with things that were meant to be respected, preserved, or clearly read — monuments, public buildings, official documents, gravestones, currency, or artworks. This is why defacing carries a strong sense of disrespect and wrongdoing.

• Public monuments and statues — perhaps the most classic example. Someone sprays graffiti on a war memorial. That memorial has been defaced.
  • Buildings and walls — painting or scratching unwanted markings onto them.
  • Currency (banknotes and coins) — writing or drawing on paper money. In many countries, this is actually illegal.
  • Official documents — crossing out text, scribbling on them, or altering their content in a way that damages their integrity or readability.
  • Road signs and notices — scratching off letters, spray-painting over them.
  • Gravestones and memorials — damaging the inscriptions or appearance of a tombstone.
  • Artworks and books — drawing on a painting or scribbling across pages of a book.
  • Websites — hackers sometimes "deface" a website by breaking in and replacing its content with unwanted images or messages. This is called website defacement and is the digital equivalent of graffiti.

The methods of defacing are as varied as the objects themselves. Common ways include:

  • Spraying paint or graffiti
  • Scratching or carving into a surface
  • Writing or drawing on something with a pen, marker, or chalk
  • Sticking stickers or posters onto something
  • Burning marks into a surface
  • Digitally altering or hacking content online

Deface vs. Destroy
These are not the same. To destroy something is to ruin it completely — to break it apart, burn it down, or make it cease to exist. To deface something is gentler in degree. The object survives, but its appearance is damaged. A building that is blown up is destroyed. A building that is spray-painted is defaced.

Deface vs. Vandalize
These two words are close cousins and are often used in similar situations, but they are not identical. Vandalize is a broader word that covers all kinds of deliberate damage to property — smashing windows, breaking furniture, slashing tires. Deface is more specific: it almost always refers to damage done to the surface or appearance of something, especially by marking or writing on it. All defacing can be called vandalism, but not all vandalism is defacing.

Deface vs. Alter
To alter something simply means to change it — and it can be neutral or even positive. To deface it means to change it in a way that damages its appearance or dignity. The negative judgment is built into the word "deface."

"Deface" is a word with a serious, disapproving tone. When you use it, you are communicating that something wrong has been done — that something of value has been disrespected. It appears frequently in news reports, legal language, and formal writing.

It is rarely, if ever, used positively. You would not say an artist "defaced" a canvas when painting a beautiful picture. The word always implies damage, disrespect, or wrongdoing.

Occasionally, yes. You might see "deface" used to describe something abstract being spoiled — for example, a lie that "defaced" someone's reputation, or poor design choices that "defaced" the beauty of a neighborhood. However, this metaphorical use is much less common than the physical one. In everyday usage, stick to the physical meaning and you will almost always be correct.

In most countries, defacing public or private property, currency, or official government documents is a criminal offense. The seriousness of the charge depends on what was defaced, how badly, and whether it was motivated by hatred (such as defacing a place of worship or a memorial). Courts and legal documents use the word "deface" frequently in these contexts.

• Vandals defaced the war memorial with red spray paint overnight.
  • It is illegal to deface currency in most countries.
  • The ancient temple was defaced when tourists carved their names into its walls.
  • Hackers defaced the company's website, replacing its homepage with a political message.
  • The historic statue was defaced beyond recognition before the police arrived.
  • He was charged with defacing public property after authorities reviewed the security footage.

To deface something is to intentionally damage or spoil its outward appearance — particularly by marking, writing on, or otherwise messing up its surface — in a way that is disrespectful, harmful, and usually illegal.
4014:
To defalcate means to secretly steal or misuse money that was entrusted to you by someone else. It is not ordinary theft. The person who defalcates is not a stranger who broke in and took something. They are someone who was given legitimate access and responsibility over money — and then betrayed that trust by taking or misusing it for their own benefit.

Think of it this way: if a stranger picks your pocket, that is theft. But if you hand your wallet to a trusted friend to hold, and they quietly help themselves to the cash inside while keeping the wallet intact — that is closer to what defalcating means.
The One Thing That Makes This Word Unique

The single most important thing to understand about "defalcate" is the pre-existing trust relationship. It is the defining feature that separates this word from general stealing.

The person who defalcates is always someone who held a position of responsibility or duty over the money — a fiduciary, in legal language. This means someone whose entire job, role, or obligation was to protect and manage those funds on behalf of others. When that person secretly takes or misuses the money, they have defalcated.

Without that trust relationship, the act is simply theft or fraud. With it, the act is defalcation — and that distinction matters enormously, especially in law.

Because the word requires a trust relationship, the people who defalcate tend to be those in positions of financial authority or care:

  • A company treasurer who skims money from the business accounts into a private account
  • A lawyer who holds client funds in a trust account and quietly uses that money for personal expenses
  • A trustee managing a deceased person's estate who pockets a portion of the inheritance instead of distributing it
  • A government official who diverts public tax money meant for a school or road project into their own pocket
  • An accountant or bookkeeper who manipulates records to hide the money they have taken from their employer
  • A fund manager who uses investors' money for their own personal benefit rather than managing it as agreed

In every single case, notice the same pattern: someone was trusted with access to money that wasn't theirs, and they abused that access.
The Scale and Nature of the Act

Defalcating is almost always a deliberate, ongoing, and concealed act. It is rarely a one-time impulsive grab. The person who defalcates typically:

  • Does it over a period of time (months or even years)
  • Takes small amounts repeatedly rather than one large sum, to avoid suspicion
  • Actively manipulates records, accounts, or documents to hide what they are doing
  • Continues until they are caught, the discrepancy is discovered, or an audit reveals the loss

This makes it a particularly serious and calculated form of wrongdoing, which is why it carries heavy legal consequences.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Defalcate" is a formal, legal, and professional word. You will almost never hear it in casual conversation. It belongs to the world of law, finance, banking, court proceedings, and formal journalism. If you read it somewhere, it is almost certainly in a legal document, a court ruling, a financial audit report, or a formal news article about financial crime.

In everyday speech, people would use words like embezzle, misappropriate, or steal from instead. But in a courtroom or a legal contract, "defalcate" is precise and carries specific weight.
How the Word Is Used — Real Examples

• "The fund manager had been defalcating client investments for over three years before the audit uncovered the losses."
  • "She was convicted of defalcating the charity's funds, having redirected nearly $200,000 into her personal accounts."
  • "The executor of the will was found to have defalcated a significant portion of the estate before the heirs became aware."
  • "He defalcated public funds that had been designated for disaster relief."

In each example, the subject had legitimate access and authority over the money — that is what makes it defalcation rather than plain theft.
The Related Words You Will Encounter

Since the word comes up in formal and legal contexts, you will often see its related forms nearby:

  • Defalcation (noun) — the act itself; the instance of misappropriating entrusted funds. "The defalcation was discovered during the annual audit."
  • Defalcator (noun) — the person who committed the act. "The defalcator had carefully falsified the records for years."

Understanding these three forms means you can handle the word in any form it takes.
One Sentence to Lock It In

If you want to remember the essence of this word forever, hold onto this:

To defalcate is to steal from the inside — by someone trusted to protect what they end up taking.

That captures everything: the trust, the betrayal, the concealment, and the seriousness of the act.
4015:
Defamation (noun) is the act of making a false statement about a person — and communicating it to others — in a way that damages that person's reputation.

That's the short version. Now let's make sure every word of that definition actually makes sense to you.
Breaking It Down, Piece by Piece

"A false statement" — This is the heart of defamation. The statement must be untrue. If someone says something negative about you that is completely true, that is not defamation, no matter how badly it hurts your reputation. Truth is an absolute shield against a defamation claim.

"About a person" — The false statement must be about a specific, identifiable person (or organization). A vague, general remark that no one can pin to a particular individual doesn't count.

"Communicated to others" — The false statement must be shared with at least one person other than the subject. If someone writes a horrible lie about you in their private diary and never shows it to anyone, that is not defamation. The damage to your reputation only happens when others hear or read it.

"Damages reputation" — Defamation isn't just about hurt feelings. The false statement must actually harm how others perceive you — for example, causing people to distrust you, fire you, avoid you, or think less of you. Reputation is the key word here.

Defamation is an umbrella term. It has two specific sub-types, depending on how the false statement is communicated:

Libel — Defamation in a written or published, permanent form. A false article in a newspaper, a damaging lie posted on social media, or a fabricated review online — these are all libel.

Slander — Defamation in a spoken, temporary form. Someone verbally spreading a false rumor about you at work, or lying about you in a conversation, is slander.

An easy way to remember: Libel = Letters (written). Slander = Spoken.
What Is NOT Defamation — This Is Crucial

Understanding what defamation is not is just as important as knowing what it is. Many people confuse the following with defamation, but they are not:

1. True statements. No matter how damaging, the truth cannot be defamation. If a journalist reports that a CEO actually did commit fraud, and it's proven to be true, the CEO has no defamation claim.

2. Opinions. Defamation requires a statement of fact — something that can be proven true or false. Pure opinions generally cannot be defamatory. There is a difference between:

  • "John is a thief" → This sounds like a fact. It can be proven true or false. Potentially defamatory if false.
  • "I think John is a terrible person" → This is an opinion. It cannot be objectively verified. Generally not defamatory.

3. Satire and parody. Exaggerated comedy or clearly fictional portrayals of public figures — like in a comedy sketch or a satirical article — are generally not defamation, because a reasonable person understands they are not meant to be taken as factual.

4. Statements made in certain protected settings. Things said during court proceedings or in government/legislative debates are often legally protected from defamation claims, so that people can speak freely in those settings without fear of lawsuits.

The law treats these two groups differently, and this is an important distinction.

Ordinary (private) people get stronger protection. If a false statement is made about you and it damages your reputation, you generally have a solid defamation claim.

Public figures — celebrities, politicians, high-profile executives — have a harder standard to meet. Because they voluntarily enter public life and must accept more scrutiny and criticism, they have to prove not just that the statement was false and damaging, but also that the person who made it knew it was false, or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true or not. This higher standard is often called "actual malice." The reason for this is to protect free speech and the press's ability to report on and criticize those in power.

• A local newspaper publishes a story falsely claiming that a restaurant owner has been poisoning customers. The story is fabricated. Customers stop visiting. The owner's business collapses. → Defamation (specifically libel).
  • A disgruntled former employee tells their new workplace colleagues that their previous manager embezzled company funds, knowing that this is completely false. The manager gets fired. → Defamation (specifically slander).
  • A film critic writes that a new movie is "the worst, most boring film ever made." The director is furious. → Not defamation. This is a subjective opinion, not a false statement of fact.
  • A journalist correctly reports that a politician accepted bribes, with solid evidence to back it up. → Not defamation. The statement is true.

The damage from defamation can be very real and wide-ranging:

  • Professional harm — job loss, destroyed career, lost clients or business
  • Social harm — damaged personal relationships, social exclusion
  • Financial harm — lost income or business opportunities
  • Emotional harm — anxiety, distress, and loss of dignity

Because of all this potential harm, most countries have laws that allow the victim of defamation to sue the person responsible and claim compensation.

If someone lies about you to other people, and that lie ruins your reputation — that is defamation. The moment you add a written or permanent form, it becomes libel. The moment it's purely spoken, it becomes slander.

The whole concept is built on one simple moral idea: you have the right to protect your reputation from deliberate or careless lies.
4016:
Something is defamatory when it damages a person's reputation by making a false statement about them that is presented as a fact — not an opinion — and that statement is shared with at least one other person.

Think of it this way: imagine someone deliberately tells your employer that you stole money from your previous job, when that never happened. That statement is defamatory. It is false, it is stated as a fact, it is shared with someone else, and it seriously harms how others see you.

So the word "defamatory" is an adjective used to describe a statement, a remark, a piece of writing, a video, or any content that meets this description.
The Four Pillars That Make Something Defamatory

For something to truly be defamatory, four conditions must be present at the same time:

It must be false. This is the most important condition. If someone says something true about you that ruins your reputation, that is not defamatory — even if it hurts you deeply. Truth is an absolute shield against defamation. If a journalist reports that a politician actually did accept a bribe, and the politician actually did, that report is not defamatory. But if the politician never accepted a bribe and the journalist says they did, that report is defamatory.

It must be stated as a fact, not an opinion. This is a crucial distinction. Saying "I think he is a dishonest person" is an expression of personal opinion, and opinions cannot be defamatory. But saying "He cheated his clients out of thousands of dollars last year" is a statement of alleged fact — something that can be checked, proven true or false — and if it is false, it is defamatory. The line between fact and opinion can sometimes be subtle, but the rule of thumb is: if a statement sounds like it could be investigated and proven true or false, it is likely treated as a statement of fact.

It must be communicated to at least one other person. If you lie about someone only to their face, with no one else around, it is not defamatory in the legal sense. The false statement must "go out" to the world — to an audience, however small. Publishing it online, saying it at a meeting, printing it in a newspaper, or even whispering it to a single colleague all count.

It must cause harm (or be likely to cause harm) to the person's reputation. The false statement must be the kind that lowers the person in the eyes of reasonable, right-thinking members of society. It must make people think less of them, distrust them, avoid them, or treat them worse than before. Saying someone "prefers tea over coffee" — even falsely — is not defamatory, because it does not damage anyone's reputation. Saying someone "committed fraud" — falsely — absolutely is.
Libel vs. Slander: Two Forms of Defamatory Content

When you come across the word "defamatory," it is worth knowing that defamatory content takes two forms:

Libel refers to defamatory content that is written, printed, or permanently recorded — a false article, a social media post, a book, a video.

Slander refers to defamatory content that is spoken aloud and is therefore temporary — a false rumour spoken in conversation, a false accusation made in a speech.

Both are defamatory; they just differ in their medium.

A gossip magazine publishes a story saying a famous surgeon was drunk while performing operations — and this is completely false. That article is defamatory.

A neighbour tells everyone in the building that you have a criminal record — and you have never been convicted of anything. That is a defamatory statement.

A former business partner sends an email to your clients saying you defrauded him — and this never happened. That email is defamatory.

Now here are examples of things that are not defamatory, even though they might feel harsh:

A critic writes that your restaurant serves "the worst pasta in the city." That is an opinion, not a statement of fact. It is not defamatory.

A news outlet reports that a company's CEO resigned amid an internal investigation — if this is actually true. True statements are never defamatory.

Someone says they "don't trust" a particular politician. That is a personal feeling, not a factual claim. Not defamatory.

The word "defamatory" is usually placed directly before a noun, or after a linking verb like "is" or "was":

"The magazine published a defamatory article about the actress."
"His comments were defamatory and could result in a lawsuit."
"She sued the website for posting defamatory content."
"The lawyer argued that the tweet was defamatory because it falsely accused her client of a crime."

Since you may encounter the entire family of words built around the same idea:

Defame is the verb — it means to make defamatory statements about someone. ("He tried to defame her by spreading lies.")
Defamation is the noun — it refers to the act or result of defaming someone. ("She filed a lawsuit for defamation.")
Defamatory is the adjective — it describes the content or statement itself. ("That was a defamatory remark.")
Defamer is the noun for the person who defames. ("The defamer was ordered to pay damages.")

Many people assume that anything mean, hurtful, or embarrassing said about someone is defamatory. It is not. The word carries a specific meaning rooted in falsehood. You can say something genuinely terrible about a person — something that destroys their career and social life — and if it is true, it is not defamatory. Defamatory is specifically about lies dressed up as facts, spread to others, in a way that damages reputation.

Another misconception is that only public attacks count. Even a false, damaging statement made in a private message to one single person can be defamatory, as long as the other conditions are met.

"Defamatory" describes any statement or content that is false, presented as a fact (not an opinion), shared with others, and harmful to someone's reputation. It is a word used both in everyday English and in legal contexts. When you see it, it signals that someone is claiming they have been lied about — publicly and damagingly.
4017:
To defame someone means to make false statements about them — to other people — that damage how others think of that person. In short, you are harming someone's reputation by spreading lies about them.

Imagine your neighbour Bob is a trusted, well-respected doctor. Now imagine someone goes around town telling people, "Bob cheated his patients out of money and faked his medical degree." None of it is true — but people start believing it. Bob loses patients, loses friends, and his good name is destroyed. The person who spread those lies has defamed Bob. They defamed him.

That is defaming — attacking someone's reputation with false information.
The three things that must be true for something to count as defaming:

1. The statement must be false.
This is the most important part. If what is said is true, it is NOT defamation — no matter how embarrassing or damaging it is. Defaming is specifically about lies presented as facts. Sharing an honest, truthful opinion is also generally not defaming (e.g., "I think his cooking is bad" is an opinion, not a false fact).

2. The statement must be communicated to at least one other person.
Calling someone a fraud to their face, privately is insulting — but it is not defaming them, because no one else heard it and no reputation was damaged. Defaming requires an audience — other people must receive the false information.

3. The statement must damage the person's reputation.
The false statement must make others think worse of the person — causing them to lose trust, respect, friends, business, or standing in society.
Two forms of defaming — same word, different delivery:

When you defame someone through spoken words, it is specifically called slander.
When you defame someone through writing, publishing, or broadcasting (a newspaper article, social media post, video, etc.), it is specifically called libel.

Both are forms of defaming. "Defame" is the umbrella term that covers both.
How it looks in real sentences:

• "The tabloid defamed the actress by falsely claiming she was involved in a crime."
  • "He sued the blogger for defaming him with made-up stories about his business."
  • "She feared that spreading those rumours would defame her colleague's career."
  • "To defame a public figure, you must prove the false statement was made with harmful intent."

• Defamation (noun) — the act of defaming someone. "He filed a lawsuit for defamation."
  • Defamatory (adjective) — describes something that defames. "The article contained defamatory lies."
  • Defamer (noun) — a person who defames someone.
To slander, to libel, to malign, to smear, to tarnish someone's reputation, to vilify, to traduce.
What defaming is NOT — sharpening the edges:

SituationIs it defaming?
You say something true that hurts someone's reputation❌ No — truth is a complete defence
You express a personal opinion ("I think she's a bad manager")❌ No — opinions are not statements of fact
You make a false statement only to that person privately❌ No — no audience means no reputation damaged
You make a false factual claim about someone to others, damaging their name✅ Yes — this is defaming
Why it matters in the real world:

Defaming someone is not just morally wrong — in most countries, it is illegal. A person who has been defamed can take the defamer to court and seek financial compensation for the damage done to their reputation, career, or personal life. This is why defamation law exists — to protect people from having their lives ruined by lies.
One-line summary to remember it forever:

To defame = to publicly damage someone's reputation by making false statements about them.

If the statement is false, factual (not just an opinion), shared with others, and harms how people see that person — someone has been defamed.
4018:
At the heart of "default" lies one simple idea: something that happens — or is treated as chosen — because nothing was done to prevent it or change it.

Think of it this way: imagine a river flowing in one direction. If you don't actively redirect it, it keeps going the same way. That "natural, uninterrupted path" is the default. You didn't choose it — it happened because no deliberate choice was made to do otherwise.

This core idea branches into two distinct families of meaning.
Meaning 1: A Failure to Do Something You Are Obligated to Do

In its oldest and most formal sense, a default is a failure to meet an obligation — especially a legal, financial, or contractual one.

The critical thing to understand here is that it is not just any failure. It is specifically a failure to do something you were required to do — something promised, agreed upon, or legally binding.

In Finance and Loans

This is the most common context you'll encounter this meaning.

When someone borrows money — say, a home loan — they are legally obligated to make monthly payments. If they stop making those payments, they are said to be in default. The moment of formally failing is called a default.

"The bank took over his house after he went into default on his mortgage."

Notice: it doesn't mean the person simply chose not to pay — it means they were supposed to pay, did not, and are now in a state of having broken that agreement.

This applies to:

  • Personal loans — failing to repay money you borrowed
  • Home loans (mortgages) — failing to make house payments
  • Credit card debt — failing to make minimum payments
  • Government debt — when a country fails to repay money it owes to other countries or institutions (this is called a sovereign default)

"Argentina experienced multiple debt defaults in the 20th century, shocking global financial markets."

The moment a default is declared, it typically triggers serious legal and financial consequences — assets may be seized, credit scores drop, legal proceedings begin.

In Law and Legal Proceedings

If a person is summoned to court and simply does not show up, the court may issue a default — meaning a judgment automatically entered against the absent party, because they failed to appear or respond.

This is sometimes called a default judgment.

"Since the defendant never responded to the lawsuit, the judge issued a default judgment in the plaintiff's favour."

Again, notice the same pattern: someone was required to do something (appear in court, file a response), they did not do it, and the consequence was automatic — it happened because nothing was done.

In Sports

If a player or team fails to show up for a match, or is disqualified for violating rules, they lose by default. The word describing that loss — or the act of forfeiting — is a default.

"The team couldn't travel due to the flood, so they had to concede a default."

The opponent wins not because they performed better, but simply because the other side was absent or unable to continue.
Meaning 2: A Pre-Set Option That Is Used When No Choice Is Made

This is the meaning you'll encounter constantly in technology, software, and everyday modern life — and it flows directly from the same core idea.

A default (in this sense) is the option, setting, or behavior that is already in place and automatically used unless someone actively changes it.

When a company builds a product — a phone, an app, a website, a document editor — they have to decide: What happens if the user never touches this setting? Whatever they pre-select becomes the default.

"The default language on the app is English, but you can switch it to Hindi in the settings."

"The default font in this word processor is Times New Roman, size 12."

"Your phone's default browser is the one it uses when you tap a link — unless you change it."

Nobody told the phone to use that browser. No one actively chose it just now. It was already set that way, and it remained because no one changed it.

Why This Meaning Matters

Understanding defaults in technology is genuinely important because they shape people's behavior without them realizing it. Research has consistently shown that most people never change default settings. This means:

  • Default privacy settings on social media determine what most people share publicly.
  • Default enrollment in pension schemes dramatically increases how many people save for retirement.
  • The default search engine a browser uses is worth billions of dollars to companies because most users never switch.

The company that gets chosen as the "default" wins an enormous advantage, simply because of human inertia — people tend not to change what's already there.

This phrase is extremely common and worth understanding deeply. It means: something came to be true not because it was actively chosen or earned, but because nothing was done to prevent it or choose otherwise.

It can apply to either major meaning of the word:

In the sense of absence/failure:

"Our team won by default — the opposing team didn't show up."

No one earned the win through skill. It was handed to them because the other side simply wasn't there.

In the sense of automatic pre-selection:

"He became the leader of the group by default — no one else wanted the job."

He wasn't elected. He wasn't the most qualified. He simply ended up in the role because no one else stepped forward.

In technology:

"The app stores your data on their servers by default."

You didn't set this up. It just happens automatically, in the background, unless you turn it off.

The phrase "by default" almost always carries a subtle undertone: this wasn't the ideal or deliberate outcome — it just happened because of absence, inaction, or a lack of better alternatives.
The Deeper Thread Connecting Both Meanings

You might wonder: how are these two meanings — "failure to pay" and "a pre-selected setting" — really the same word?

They share a common logic:

Both describe what happens when no active, deliberate action is taken.

  • In the financial/legal sense: when you fail to act (fail to pay, fail to appear), the default is what kicks in — the consequence.
  • In the technological sense: when you fail to choose (don't touch the settings), the default is what kicks in — the pre-selected option.

In both cases, the default is the automatic outcome of inaction. It is what the world does with you when you don't direct it yourself.

Understanding which words "default" commonly travels with will sharpen your feel for it:

  • Go into default / fall into default — to reach the state of having missed obligatory payments
  • Default on a loan — to fail to repay as agreed (here "default" is also used as a verb, but the idea is the same)
  • Default judgment — a legal ruling made because one party didn't respond or appear
  • Default settings — the settings that come pre-loaded on a device or app
  • Default option — the choice that is automatically selected
  • In default of — a more formal phrase meaning "in the absence of" or "due to the failure of"

    "In default of a will, the estate was divided according to law."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

ContextWhat "default" means

In financial and legal contexts, a default is the state of having failed to meet an obligation — a missed payment, a broken contract, an absent defendant. It is serious, often triggering legal or financial consequences.

In technology and everyday contexts, a default is a pre-set, automatically-chosen option that applies unless someone deliberately changes it. It requires no action from you — it simply is, until overridden.

In both cases, "by default" means something came to be true through the absence of deliberate choice or action — either because someone failed to do what they should have, or because no one actively selected an alternative.

That's the word in full.
4019:
Defeatism is an attitude — a way of thinking — in which a person accepts that they are going to fail or lose, often before the outcome has even been decided, and sometimes without putting up a real fight. It is the mindset of someone who has mentally given up.

Think of it this way: imagine you are about to take a difficult exam. A defeatist attitude would be saying to yourself, "There's no point in studying. I'm going to fail anyway." You haven't taken the exam yet. You don't know the result. But in your mind, you have already lost — and because of that belief, you stop trying. That is defeatism.
What makes it "defeatism" and not just feeling nervous or discouraged?

Everyone feels doubt sometimes. That's normal. What separates defeatism from ordinary doubt or worry is this: a defeatist doesn't just feel that failure is possible — they accept it as certain, and that acceptance causes them to stop resisting, stop fighting, or stop trying altogether. The belief in defeat becomes so strong that it drives their behavior.

This is important, because defeatism often becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy — meaning the defeatist's attitude causes the very failure they were afraid of, because they stopped making the effort that could have prevented it.

There are three things happening when someone falls into defeatism:

1. A premature conclusion. The person decides the outcome is already known — that failure is unavoidable — even though the situation hasn't fully played out yet. They give up in advance.

2. A surrender of effort. Because they believe defeat is inevitable, they see no reason to keep trying, resisting, or pushing forward. The fight leaves them — mentally, if not physically.

3. A harmful effect on others (often). Defeatism rarely stays contained to one person. When someone voices defeatist views — "We can't win this," "There's no hope," "Why bother?" — it can drag down the morale of an entire group, team, army, or community.

The word can be used in many contexts:

  • In war or conflict: A general who tells his troops, "The enemy is too powerful; we have already lost," is spreading defeatism. He hasn't lost yet — but his attitude ensures that his army will stop fighting with full effort, making defeat far more likely.
  • In politics: A candidate who tells supporters mid-campaign, "Our opponents are unbeatable, so don't bother voting," is being defeatist. The election hasn't happened. That attitude suppresses effort and action.
  • In business: A company leader who says, "The market has changed; there's nothing we can do; our competitors will always beat us," and then stops innovating — that is defeatism in a business context.
  • In personal life: A student who says, "People like me don't get into good universities," and therefore doesn't apply, is being defeatist. They accepted defeat without even trying.
  • In social or political change: A group of people who say, "Injustice will never change, so why protest or organize?" are expressing defeatism. They have given up on the possibility of improvement before making a genuine effort.
How defeatism differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Defeatism vs. Pessimism: Pessimism is a general tendency to expect bad outcomes in life — a gloomy worldview overall. Defeatism is more specific — it is focused on a particular struggle, challenge, or contest, and it involves not just expecting to lose but accepting the loss and abandoning effort. A pessimist might still try, even while expecting failure. A defeatist has, in some sense, already stopped trying in their heart.

Defeatism vs. Realism: A realist looks at a difficult situation and honestly acknowledges the challenges. Crucially though, a realist doesn't necessarily give up — they might work harder because they see the obstacles clearly. A defeatist goes one step further: they conclude that the challenges are insurmountable and that further effort is pointless.

Defeatism vs. Surrender: Surrender is an action — you physically or formally give up. Defeatism is the mental attitude that usually comes before surrender, or that exists without ever formally surrendering. You can be a defeatist and still be "in the fight" physically, while having mentally checked out entirely.
The tone and connotation of the word

Defeatism is almost always used as a criticism. When someone accuses another person of defeatism, they are saying: "You are giving up too easily. You are hurting our chances of success by accepting defeat before it has happened. Your attitude is the problem, not the situation itself."

It implies a lack of resilience, courage, or fighting spirit. It suggests that the person is choosing to surrender mentally when they still had a real chance.

However, it's worth noting that not every accusation of defeatism is fair. Sometimes people are called defeatists simply for being honest about very difficult odds — for telling the truth that a situation is genuinely bleak. When that happens, the word is being used as a silencing tactic: "Stop being negative," when the person is actually just being truthful. Understanding the word deeply means recognizing this tension — between the genuine problem of giving up too soon, and the misuse of the word to shut down honest, realistic assessment.
The related forms of the word

• Defeatist (as a noun): a person who practices or expresses defeatism. "Don't listen to him — he's a defeatist. He said we'd lose before the game even started."
  • Defeatist (as an adjective): describing an attitude, thought, or remark that reflects defeatism. "That's a defeatist way of thinking."
  • Defeatism (the noun you asked about): the attitude or belief system itself.

If you ever need to recall this quickly: Defeatism is the attitude of accepting failure as inevitable — before it has actually happened — in a way that causes a person to stop trying, and often causes the very defeat they feared.
